documentNotes.title: Native editorial preface
documentNotes.statement:
Preface
Preface
Preface
Preface 
This publication contains the competition problems (Volume 2) from the 21st – 40th 
International Chemistry Olympiads (IChO) organized in the years 1989 – 2008  and is a 
continuation of the publication that appeared last year as Volume 1 and contained 
competition problems from the first twenty IChOs.  The whole review of the competition 
tasks set in the IChO in its fourty-year history is a contribution of the IChO International 
Information Centre in Bratislava (Slovakia) to the development of this world known 
international competition. This Volume 2 contains 154 theoretical and 46 practical 
competition problems from the mentioned years. The review as a whole presents 
altogether 279 theoretical and 96 practical problems.  
In the elaboration of this collection the editor had to face certain difficulties because 
the aim was not only to make use of past recordings but also to give them such a form 
that they may be used in practice and further chemical education. Consequently, it was 
necessary to make some corrections in order to unify the form of the problems. However, 
they did not concern the contents and language of the problems.  
Unfortunately, the authors of the particular competition problems are not known and 
due to the procedure of the creation of the IChO competition problems, it is impossible to 
assign any author's name to a particular problem. As the editor I would appreciate many  
times some discussion with the authors about any critical places that occurred in the text. 
On the other hand, any additional amendments to the text would be not correct from the  
historical point of view. Therefore, responsibility for the scientific content and language of 
the problems lies exclusively with the organizers of the particular International Chemistry 
Olympiads.    
 
Some parts of texts, especially those gained as scanned materials, could not be 
used directly and thus, several texts, schemes and pictures had to be re-written or created 
again. Some solutions were often available in a brief form and necessary extent only, just 
for the needs of members of the International Jury.  
 
Recalculations of the solutions were made in some special cases only when the 
numeric results in the original solutions showed to be obviously not correct. Although the 
numbers of significant figures in the results of several solutions do not obey the criteria 
generally accepted, they were left without change.      


 
In this publication SI quantities and units are used and a more modern method of 
chemical calculations is introduced. Only some exceptions have been made when, in an 
effort to preserve the original text, the quantities and units have been used that are not SI.  
There were some problems with the presentation of the solutions of practical tasks, 
because most of the relatively simple calculations were based on the experimental results 
of contestants. Moreover, the practical problems are accompanied with answer sheets in 
the last years and several additional questions and tasks have appeared in them that were 
not a part of the text of the original experimental problems. Naturally, answer sheets could 
not be included in this publication and can only be preserved as archive materials. 
  
When reading the texts of the IChO problems one must admire and appreciate the 
work of those many known and unknown people – teachers, authors, pupils, and 
organizers – who contributed so much to development and success of this important 
international competition. 
 
I am sure about the usefulness of the this review of the IChO problems. It may serve 
not only as archive material but, in particular, this review should serve to both competitors 
and their teachers as a source of further inspiration in their preparation for this challenging 
competition. 
 
 
 
 
Bratislava, July 2009  
 
 
 
 
 
 
  
 
                                    Anton Sirota, editor

problems.title: problem 1

sections.title: Effects of carbon dioxide on solubility
sections.statement:
Calcium carbonate is a partially soluble material known as limestone, marble, chalk or calcite. It dissolves in carbon-dioxide-rich groundwater, forming cavities and caves in limestone.

Determine the solubility of calcium carbonate in aqueous solution saturated with carbon dioxide and in carbon-dioxide-free solution. Determine $[\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}]$ by complexometric titration with EDTA, ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid.

sections.title: Procedure
sections.statement:
### a) Determination of $[\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}]$

1. Calibrate the pH meter.
2. Measure and record the pH of the sample equilibrated with solid $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ and gaseous $\mathrm{CO_2}$.
3. Filter the whole sample into a second $250\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ plastic bottle to remove suspended calcium carbonate. Cap quickly after filtering.
4. Uncap only long enough to measure and record the filtered solution's pH. Recap until the next step.
5. Quickly transfer three $25\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ aliquots to three Erlenmeyer flasks, recapping after each aliquot.
6. Stir $15$ drops of $6\ \mathrm M$ HCl into each flask. Any calcium carbonate formed should dissolve. Ensure no solid remains before continuing; if necessary stir more.
7. To one flask only, add $5\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of pH $10$ ammonia buffer. Immediately continue with steps 8–10.
8. Add $20$ drops of $0.001\ \mathrm M$ $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}/EDTA^{4-}}$ solution so the indicator functions properly.
9. Add five drops of Calmagite indicator.
10. Titrate with the approximately $0.01\ \mathrm M$ EDTA solution, to be standardized below, until red changes to blue. A colour reference may be made from water, buffer, two drops of EDTA and indicator.
11. Quickly repeat steps 7–10 for each remaining flask, one at a time.
12. After completing steps 1–11 satisfactorily, transfer the remaining filtered saturated solution from step 3 to a suitable beaker. Heat to $96$–$99\,{}^\circ\mathrm C$, with magnetic stirring, for five minutes. Stirrer setting 6 is adequate; initially a high heat setting is needed. Carbon dioxide should evolve and calcium carbonate may precipitate.
13. After five minutes, remove the beaker from the hot plate with beaker tongs and place it in an ice bath. Cool to room temperature.
14. Measure and record the cooled solution's pH.
15. Filter to remove suspended calcium carbonate.
16. Transfer three $25\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ aliquots to three Erlenmeyer flasks. Add about $25\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of deionized water and then $15$ drops of $6\ \mathrm M$ HCl to each.
17. Titrate each sample according to steps 7–11.

### b) Standardization of EDTA

1. Weigh approximately $0.35\ \mathrm g$ of dried primary-standard $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$, molar mass $100.09\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$, from the weighing bottle in the desiccator. The native note says: “CaCO₃ is hygroscopic.”
2. Add $25\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of deionized water, then carefully add $5\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of $6\ \mathrm M$ HCl. Cover quickly with a watch glass.
3. When the solid dissolves, quantitatively transfer to a $250\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ volumetric flask and dilute to the mark.
4. Transfer three $25\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ aliquots of standard calcium-ion solution to three Erlenmeyer flasks.
5. Titrate each according to steps 7–11, in sequence.

parts.statement: Calculate calcium carbonate solubility in $\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ in a solution saturated with both $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ and $\mathrm{CO_2}$, and in a carbon-dioxide-free solution.
List all ionic species whose concentration increases when calcium carbonate dissolves in water.

Circle the solution having the greater carbonate-ion concentration:

a) Calcium carbonate dissolved in carbon-dioxide-saturated water.

b) Calcium carbonate dissolved in carbon-dioxide-free water.
Does calcium carbonate solubility increase or decrease when carbon dioxide is removed?

sections.statement: The answer sheet must contain titrant volumes, the calcium carbonate mass and the calculation of standardized EDTA concentration. Record pH values from steps 2, 4 and 14. Show calcium carbonate solubility calculations for saturated solutions with and without carbon dioxide.
Correct answer: b), calcium carbonate dissolved in carbon-dioxide-free water.

solution.incompleteReason:
The separate answer sheet and actual titration volumes, calcium carbonate mass and pH measurements are absent from these obtained pages. No numerical solubility or measured entries are invented. The source's hygroscopicity note is retained; its 1.2 ionic-species list omits carbonate although 1.3 separately asks about carbonate concentration. Both complete procedures, all four connected tasks and the printed key remain one whole experiment.
